title: Love your neighbor (Leviticus 19:9–18)
hook: leave the edges of the field for the poor; love your neighbor as yourself

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bezalel, the craftsman filled with the spirit of God. Your line was craft is spiritual. What did you do slowly and well? Day four hundred one.

Leviticus can be slow going: sacrifices, skin diseases, mildew, priestly clothing. And then, in the middle of it, chapter nineteen. A farmer is bringing in the harvest. The sickles swing through the wheat, row after row, and when they reach the corners of the field, they stop. On purpose. They leave the corners standing. Behind them, a few stalks have fallen to the ground, and nobody goes back to pick them up. In the vineyard, a few grapes have dropped, and they're left lying there too. It looks like sloppy farming. It's actually the law.
screen: `LEVITICUS: SLOW GOING?` → `THE SICKLES STOP AT THE CORNERS.` → `THE FALLEN STALKS STAY DOWN.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "thou shalt not wholly reap the corners of thy field, neither shalt thou gather the gleanings of thy harvest." And the grapes too: "thou shalt leave them for the poor and stranger: I am the LORD your God." It's welfare built into the field itself. The poor don't have to beg at the farmhouse door. They walk into the field and gather what was left for them, with their own hands, with dignity. That's exactly how Ruth, a poor foreign widow, ends up gleaning in the field of Boaz, a story the path reaches next year. The Jewish oral law later gave a whole tractate of the Mishnah to these corners, called Peah, corner. Then chapter nineteen keeps going, line after line, all ordinary life. Don't hold back a worker's wages overnight. "Thou shalt not curse the deaf, nor put a stumblingblock before the blind." Don't spread gossip. Don't stand idle while your neighbor's life is in danger. Don't hate your brother in your heart. Don't take revenge or bear a grudge. And then, at the end of the list, almost tucked in: "but thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself: I am the LORD." This is the line Jesus will quote as the second great commandment, straight from Leviticus. And look at the shape of the chapter. Love your neighbor isn't a warm feeling floating in the air. It's corners of fields, wages paid on time, the deaf and the blind protected, grudges dropped. Love has edges you can see. And later in the same chapter, the law says the stranger among you is to be loved as yourself too.
screen: `DON'T REAP THE CORNERS.` · `THE POOR GLEAN WITH DIGNITY.` · `NO GRUDGES, NO STUMBLING BLOCKS.` · `THE LINE JESUS WILL QUOTE.` · then, large: `“THOU SHALT LOVE THY NEIGHBOUR AS THYSELF.”`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: leave something for others. Settle, and breathe. Picture your own field: your paycheck, your pantry, your time, your parking spot, the last slice, the best seat. Where are the corners? Where could you stop the sickle a little early and leave something standing, without making a speech about it? Maybe a few dollars where someone will find them. The good parking space. An hour of your week. Choose one corner. Picture someone else gathering it. If you pray, you can pray for whoever will. The bell holds the time.
Peah. Hebrew for corner, the Mishnah's name for the harvest law: leaving the edges of the field standing for the poor and the stranger.
Your line: leave the edges. Today, don't take all of something: leave the last of it, quietly, for someone else to find. Day four hundred one.

howItsDone: Christians learn 'love thy neighbour as thyself' as the second great commandment, and some churches and farms practice modern gleaning, gathering leftover crops after harvest for food banks.

fork.setup: you're a farmer bringing in the harvest. the sickles reach the corners of the field. what does the law say?
options: reap it all; you planted it.
stop, and leave the corners standing.

fork.reveal: leave the corners and the gleanings "for the poor and stranger". the field itself is built to feed people.

original.note: Hebrew: and you shall love your neighbor as yourself (Leviticus 19:18).

trapdoor: what you thought: a nice saying from Jesus.
what it means: a line from Leviticus, at the end of a list of very concrete kindnesses: corners left, wages paid, grudges dropped.
what a scholar hears: Leviticus 19:18, with 19:34 stretching it to the stranger; the corners became a whole Mishnah tractate, Peah.
